American poetry. The diverse and evolving poetic traditions developed in the United States, from colonial-era devotional verse through contemporary experimental work. American poets have drawn inspiration from romanticism and modernism and indigenous voices to forge a distinctive tradition that emphasizes individualism and democratic energy and formal innovation. Figures like Hart Crane and Allen Ginsberg exemplify the movement's range and its commitment to pushing the boundaries of language.

Early American poetry was deeply influenced by British Romanticism and Transcendentalism, particularly Ralph Waldo Emerson and Henry David Thoreau. The nineteenth century saw the emergence of distinctly American voices, including Emily Dickinson's experimental metrics and Walt Whitman's expansive free verse. Hart Crane's modernist epics synthesized American industrial imagery and classical mythology and formally daring language to capture the American landscape and psyche. Allen Ginsberg's Howl from nineteen fifty-six became an anthem of the Beat Generation, combining long prophetic lines and autobiographical intensity and social protest.

American poetry encompasses diverse regional and cultural traditions: African American poetry and Chicano poetry and Native American poetry and immigrant poetic voices, each enriching the mainstream. The Harlem Renaissance produced canonical African American poets exploring racial identity and jazz aesthetics and modernist form. Contemporary American poetry remains experimental and plural, with no single dominant school. Poets draw on confessional and language and slam and mixed-media traditions.

American poetry prizes colloquial speech and personal experience and formal innovation, often rejecting the high formality associated with British tradition. The relationship between technical precision and accessibility remains a defining tension in American poetry. Poetry itself is the art form, and American poetry is a major regional and historical branch of it. Hart Crane was a modernist poet whose visionary epics explored American identity and landscape. Allen Ginsberg was a Beat poet and countercultural figure. Howl remains a touchstone of twentieth-century American literature. Walt Whitman was the nineteenth-century revolutionary whose expansive free verse shaped all American poetry after him. Emily Dickinson was a reclusive nineteenth-century poet whose innovative metrics anticipated modernism. The Harlem Renaissance saw the flowering of African American poetic voices in the early twentieth century.
